walkthroughs.body_html:
Internal Assessment: Historical Investigation — a core area of History.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Internal Assessment: Historical Investigation brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Internal Assessment: Historical Investigation.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which Bolshevik slogan summarised Lenin's April Theses?
options: Peace, Land, Bread
Workers of the world unite
Liberte, egalite, fraternite
Better dead than red

mcqs.q: What was the immediate cause of the February Revolution?
options: German invasion
Bread shortages in Petrograd
Lenin's return from Switzerland
Kerensky's offensive

mcqs.q: Why did William of Normandy claim the English throne in 1066?
options: William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.
He claimed Edward the Confessor had promised him the throne in 1051 and that Harold Godwinson had sworn an oath to support that claim in 1064.
William invaded because he was the strongest king in Europe and wanted more land.
Railways were transformative because they were the first form of public transport.

mcqs.q: Why were railways transformative for Victorian Britain?
options: William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.
Railways were transformative mainly because they were faster than horses.
Railways were transformative because they were the first form of public transport.
They cut transport costs and times, integrated national markets, enabled commuting and mass leisure travel, and standardised time zones — reshaping economy and society after 1830.

mcqs.q: How was crime punished in Anglo-Saxon England?
options: Railways were transformative because they were the first form of public transport.
Through wergild ('man-price') compensation for victims, communal responsibility via tithings, trial by ordeal in disputed cases, and the death penalty for serious crimes.
Anglo-Saxons punished all crimes with imprisonment in castle dungeons.
Anglo-Saxons had no laws and just took revenge on each other.
